newsitem.title: UK: Eurobonds tap Greek drachma and kiwi dollars.
newsitem.headline: Eurobonds tap Greek drachma and kiwi dollars.

text.p: 1130 GMT - A handful of interesting deals were launched in the Eurobond market on Tuesday.
** New Zealand dollars, dormant since early July, saw the World Bank launch a NZ$600 million 10-year zero-coupon bond.
** The Greek drachma sector saw its third deal in a week, with the IFC launching a 27.5 billion drachma five-year FRN.
** Sanwa Business Credit Corp made it debut in the public Eurobond market with a $200 million five-year FRN.
DETAILS AND BACKGROUND FOLLOW
Eurobonds saw a handful of interesting deals on Tuesday aimed at particular niches of the market.

The New Zealand dollar sector saw its first transaction in a month, with the World Bank launching a NZ$600 million 10-year zero-coupon bond. The deal will be priced later to yield five basis points over the kiwi dollar government bond curve.

An official at lead manager TD Securities said U.S. and European investors were positive on the long-end of the market, which has an inverted yield curve, but were concerned about currency volatility.
The zero-coupon structure increases duration, thus amortising the cost of currency hedging, he said.
"We have seen very good take-up and essentially sold out on our side," the official said.

"We would have done NZ$1.0 billion if we could have got the swap. NZ$600 million is the largest 10-year swap the market has seen for a long time. Imagine that spreads will now compress and that will limit further issuance, but the idea is a good one and might be subject to a copycat transaction," he said.

The neighbouring Australian market also saw a new issue, with State Bank of New South Wales launching a A$100 million December 2001 bond, the only primary deal apart from last week's Fannie Mae global.
The drop in Aussie dollar yields, compounded by last week's rate cut, has led to a sharp fall in Eurobond retail demand for the currency, bankers said.
"The borrower is a top credit in the sector, and the deal should go well," a specialist said.
"However, there is not much going on in the sector because yields at the short end are through Treasuries. Redemptions will be re-invested in U.S. dollars, or New Zealand dollars," he said.
Kiwi yields are three years are 7.10 percent, versus 6.0 percent in the U.S. At two years, they are 7.30 percent and 5.89 percent respectively.

Further high-yield business was seen in the Greek drachma sector, where the International Finance Corp set a 27.5 billion drachma five-year FRN. The deal follows two transactions in the sector last week, which were driven by expectations that Greek yields will drop.
"European investors are attracted to the high yields available, the likelihood of yield convergence with Europe and the stability of the drachma," a Eurobond trader said.
Greek 10-year government bonds yield nearly four percentage points more than German and French paper, and 3-1/4 points more than 10-year U.S. Treasury notes.

In the mainstream market, Sanwa Business Credit Corp launched a $200 million five-year FRN, its debut public Eurobond market financing. Rated AA3/A-, SBCC has a keepwell agreement from Japan's Sanwa Bank Ltd.
The deal was pre-marketed and bonds had been placed by the time of launch, an official at joint lead manager Merrill Lynch said.
The bond was priced to yield 25 basis points over Libor, and was trading at this reoffer spread after it was freed to trade.
"There are very few corporate issues in the market which offer spreads above 20 b.p. over Libor," the Merrill Lynch official said.
Outstanding dollar FRNs include a GMAC April 2002, trading at 16 b.p. over Libor and a Nationsbank June 2002 trading at 13 b.p. over.

Bankers said SBCC's lack of name recognition, and the "Japan premium" required by investors worried about the creditworthiness of Japanese banks, meant Tuesday's issue paid more. -- Aline van Duyn, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7748
